newsitem.title: UK: Britain's main parties promise a "better Britain".
newsitem.headline: Britain's main parties promise a "better Britain".

text.p: For Prime Minister John Major, 18 years of Conservative rule has created a "better Britain". His aim this time, he writes in the ruling party's manifesto for the May 1 election is to make Britain "the best place in the world".

For Tony Blair, the Labour leader tipped by polls to oust Major and take power after the election, the unbroken stretch of Conservative government has been a very mixed blessing, with some improvements but with the majority of people left out.
"Our case is simple: that Britain can and must be better," says Blair in a glossy, 40-page Labour manifesto.
Despite the similarity of language, both parties present what they say is a radically different plans of action.
Blair made 10 commitments in what he called a "contract with the people", while Major offered 25 "pledges for the nation".
But commentators say Labour's move to the centre has drastically narrowed the gap between the parties.
Here is a comparison of the main promises in the manifestos.
TAX AND SPENDING

- The Conservatives promise "tight control of public spending priorities, aiming for our target of a 20p (20 percent) basic rate of income tax over the next parliament". The party also promises to stick to low inflation policies. In a manifesto surprise, Major offered tax breaks for families where one partner is looking after children or relatives, by allowing them to switch unused personal tax allowances to the working partner.

- Labour pledges no increases in the basic or top rates of tax, with an "objective" of a 10p (10 percent) starting rate -- although there is no target date for this to be achieved. It will also set "tough" targets for inflation and keep within the government's published spending levels. Labour dismissed Major's "family tax break", saying the costs had not been worked out.
EDUCATION

- Major's manifesto promises more independence for schools, creating a "grammar school" -- schools geared towards academic performance with a significant proportion of pupils selected by aptitude -- in every town. It also promises more rigorous appraisal of teachers, targets for school performance and more information for parents on the performance of schools.

- Blair's "Number One priority". Labour would boost nursery education, cut class sizes in primary schools, set minimum standards for homework and improve teacher training -- while closing down failing schools. Money would gradually be pumped in, but only as it became available from a declining social security budget. Grammar schools would be left, but the assisted places scheme, which pays private school fees for a limited number of high-achieving pupils who cannot afford it, would go.
JOBS
- Major says staying out of the European Union's Social Chapter will protect jobs and promises to continue a scheme requiring the long-term unemployed to go on work experience.

- Blair promises to get 250,000 young unemployed off benefit and into work through a jobs scheme funded by a "windfall tax" on privatised utilities like water, gas and electricity firms -- the only spending commitment of a manifesto designed to bury the party's old reputation as a "tax and spend" party.
HEALTH

- Major promises to increase the real resources given to the National Health Service and bring new investment in from the private sector, while boosting local treatment with a broader range of services offered through local doctor's surgeries.
- Labour is pledging to cut the money spent on administration, channelling it instead to patient care.
LAW AND ORDER

- The Conservatives, traditionally the party of law and order but watching its lead in this area slip away, promises a crack-down on petty crime, more closed circuit television cameras in town centres and automatic life sentences for anyone convicted of a second serious sexual or violent crime.
- Labour, in Blair's words, promises to be "tough on crime and tough on the causes of crime" as well as halving the time it takes to take persistent juvenile offenders to court.
WELFARE

- The Conservatives promise a crackdown on welfare cheats, as well as major reforms to the pension system, with all young people coming into the workforce paying into a personal pension fund. There will also be changes to ensure old people can insure against the cost of care in old age.

- Labour would retain the state old-age pension, while creating second pensions for those on low and modest incomes and setting up a Royal Commission to work out a fair system for funding long-term care for the elderly. Blair said all the details had not been worked out but said this was better than the "panic thinking" of the Conservatives.
POLITICS
- Major, warning that Labour's plans would lead to the break-up of the United Kingdom, promises an "evolutionary -- rather than revolutionary -- approach to constitutional change.

- Blair, capitalising on sleaze allegations which have dogged Major, wants reforms to clean up politics and show where political donations come from, to reform the House of Lords and to devolve power to Scotland and Wales through referendums offering the people of those countries seperate assemblies.
EUROPE AND FOREIGN POLICY

- In perhaps the most distinct policy of the whole manifesto, Major pledged not to allow Britain to become part of a federal European state, maintaining the country's veto and border controls, and keeping his options open on whether or not to join a single currency, joining only in the life of the next parliament after a referendum.

Although promising a referendum if a Labour government decides to enter a single currency, Blair promises to make Britain take a central role in Europe, signing the Social Chapter and forging alliances with other states to enlarge the European Union and reform the Common Agricultural Policy, while retaining a veto over key areas like border controls.
